Project work
Structure :
Each group to be between 4 to 5 students in a group, and a short personal reﬂection by each student.

Questions :
1. How may you maximise the use of structured data currently collected within your organisation? In
your response, please state the industry and geographies the organisation is in, the data collected,
ways in which you propose to maximise the use of data and provide a cost-beneﬁt analysis. Determine
the data risks involved and any mitigating actions to be taken and by whom.

2. It is said that data is the key enabler of innovation and digitalisation, for example Generative AI.
Critically examine the importance of good quality data in supporting these initiatives. Provide clear
examples of the type of data that support the type of innovation and the ﬁnancial values they bring.
Additionally, determine the roles and responsibilities of various parties involved to ensure the quality
of the data in your selected use case for innovation. Also, determine the pitfalls of poor quality data
and the potential causes of these, and how they should be remediated.

[Slide image transcription] From the regulators' desk - BCBS 239 Principles (Effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting). 1 Governance and oversight: clear roles, responsibilities and effective oversight for risk data aggregation and reporting. 2 Data architecture and IT infrastructure: robust and flexible architecture and infrastructure to support risk data needs. 3 Data accuracy and integrity: accurate, complete, consistent and reliable risk data. 4 Data completeness: all material risk data captured across legal entities, business lines, products and geographies. 5 Data consistency: consistent data definitions and data standards across the organisation. 6 Data timeliness: risk data available within required timelines to meet management and supervisory needs. 7 Adaptability: able to respond to changes in risk profile, business environment and supervisory requirements. 8 Data aggregation capability: aggregate risk data across legal entities, business lines, products and geographies on a timely basis. 9 Risk reporting practices: comprehensive reporting practices that provide accurate, clear and insightful information. 10 Frequency of risk reporting: appropriate reporting frequency to meet internal and supervisory needs. 11 Content of risk reports: include forward-looking, current and historical information, and cover all material risks. 12 Accuracy of risk reports: risk reports are accurate and reflect the underlying risk data. 13 Clarity and usefulness: information presented in a clear, concise and actionable manner for intended users. 14 Independent review: regular independent review of risk data aggregation and risk reporting, with findings reported to the board.

CBIRC regulations and ﬁndings

[Slide image transcription] CBIRC regulations and findings. The CBIRC has taken steps to enforce its guidelines. In April alone: 8 banks were fined for violating guidelines; 17.7m CNY penalties in total; penalties for each bank ranged from CNY1.6m to CNY2.7m. Reasons for the fines - banks were fined for under-reporting or inaccurate reporting of: client information, regulatory reports, interbank transactions, trade finance transactions, wealth/AUM volume, securitised asset transactions, loans write-off amounts. How did CBIRC perform its checks? CBIRC used an inspection analysis system (Examination & Analysis System Technology, EAST) which includes modules such as standardised models for data collection and extraction, on-site inspection management, data modelling tools, data model release and management. Disciplinary actions against banking executives in April: 75% received warnings (77), 18% prohibited from banking roles (19), 6% disqualified from senior executive roles (6).

[Slide image transcription] Data management structure - pros and cons. Decentralized: Business Units operate with complete autonomy, with no central control (examples shown: BHP, UPS, Visa, Nike, Google). Pros: BUs have complete autonomy and flexibility; quick decision making at BU level. Cons: disjointed, duplicated efforts; inconsistent quality across BUs; inability to cross-leverage capacity, skills and best practices. Trending away from decentralised: implement enterprise-wide governance; align resources with strategic needs; establish formal talent management. Federated (Hub and Spoke): central + selective localized capability distribution, with centralized control (examples: P&G, GSK, Amazon, Bank of Ireland). Pros: better Business-IT integration; easy to cross-pollinate capacity, skills and best practices; better efficiency and minimal duplication. Cons: slower decision making due to distributed ownership and larger stakeholder groups. Leading practice: consolidate decentralized / centralized structures into a hub-and-spoke; maintain central control, with local flexibility and niche talent. Centralized: single point of control at enterprise level, with BUs selectively engaged (examples: Capital One, HSBC, Coca-Cola, Rio Tinto). Pros: faster decision making; greater data consistency across BUs; better efficiency and minimal duplication. Cons: low agility and collaboration; transactional engagement, strategic misalignment between central and local teams. Trending away from centralised: empower local decision making; align specialty talent with functional needs; encourage broader data innovation.

What is Data Architecture?
Definition of Data Architecture
Data architecture is a bridge between the requirements for data of the business process and the physical execution of that data
in technology infrastructure. It defines data models such as taxonomies and ontologies as well as data domains, metadata,
and business critical data to execute processes across the data control environment.

Definition of Technology Architecture
Technology architecture determines how data, tools and platforms operate in collaboration to satisfy business requirements.
The proper alignment of these components dictates application efficiency and system processing speed. This enables
organizations to control costs and achieve infrastructure scalability and elasticity which are characteristic of an organization that
is designed for long-term implementation success.

Introducing controls over data in cloud

[Slide image transcription] Introducing controls over data in cloud (EDMC's CDMC Key Controls and Automation). 14 key controls in 6 areas. 1.0 Governance & Accountability: (1) Data Control Compliance metric derived from all CDMC key controls must be produced for all data assets containing sensitive data; (2) Ownership field in a data catalog must be populated for all sensitive data; (3) A register of Authoritative Sources and Authorized Distributors must be populated for all data assets containing sensitive data; (4) Data Sovereignty and Cross-Border Movement of sensitive data must be recorded, auditable and controlled according to defined policy. 2.0 Cataloguing & Classification: (5) Cataloguing must be automated for all data at point of creation or ingestion; (6) Classification must be automated for all data at point of creation or ingestion and must be always on. 3.0 Accessibility & Usage: (7) Entitlements and Access for sensitive data must be defaulted to creator and owner and access must be tracked for all sensitive data; (8) Data Consumption Purpose must be provided for all Data Sharing Agreements involving sensitive data. 4.0 Protection & Privacy: (9) Appropriate Security Controls must be enabled for sensitive data and evidence must be recorded; (10) Data Privacy Impact Assessments must be automatically triggered for all personal data according to its jurisdiction. 5.0 Data Lifecycle: (11) Data Quality Measurement must be enabled for sensitive data with metrics distributed when available; (12) Data Retention, Archiving and Purging must be managed according to a defined retention schedule. 6.0 Data & Technical Architecture: (13) Data Lineage information must be available for all sensitive data; (14) Cost Metrics directly associated with the use, storage and movement of data must be available in the catalog.

[Slide image transcription] ASEAN Data Management Framework (data governance and protection throughout the data lifecycle). 6 foundational components of the DMF, which aim to enable the organisation to leverage on a corporate governance structure to define, manage and monitor its data management processes: 1 Governance and oversight - provide direction for employees across the organisation in implementing and executing the DMF and oversee the function to confirm it is operating as designed. 2 Policies and procedural documents - develop data management policies and procedures based on the DMF throughout the data lifecycle, to ensure a clear mandate within the organisation. 3 Data inventory - identify and gather the data used and collected as well as storage type, so as to enable understanding of data taxonomy and data purpose. 4 Impact / Risk assessment - assess the impact using different impact categories if confidentiality (C), integrity (I) or availability (A) parameters are compromised. 5 Controls - design and implement protection controls within the systems according to the categories assigned and data lifecycle. 6 Monitoring and continuous improvement - monitor, measure, analyse and evaluate the DMF components implemented to keep it up-to-date and optimised.

[Slide image transcription] When does data become an asset? Data value drivers: Completeness - generally, the more complete a dataset, the more valuable it is, as it reduces bias; completeness has to be determined subject to the use case. Consistency - data is consistent if it conforms to the syntax of its definition. Accuracy - the degree to which data correctly describes the 'real world'; provenance is a critical aspect of accuracy, as it lets the user understand the history of the data and account for errors. Timeliness - the more timely and up-to-date the data is, the more valuable it is; however, timeliness is a relative measure dependent on the use case intended. Exclusivity - the more unique the dataset, the more valuable the data is; the extent of the impact of exclusivity on value is dependent on the use case. Usage Restrictions - the less restricted the use of the shared data is, the higher its value. Liability and Risks - potential liability and risks associated with the data shared could reduce its value. Interoperability/Accessibility - all things being equal, a consumer will choose the most accessible dataset; interoperability or joinability of the data is often critical for the consumer to use the data. Usefulness: the value of data lies in its usefulness; data without concrete or potential application has no inherent value; data value drivers are the key underlying factors that drive usefulness of data.
